Four maps of the same country, 1855 to 2022. The shaded area is land held by Native American nations.

How the West became confetti — a thread 🧵🗺️

1/ 1855: the shading covers most of the interior West. This was treaty land. The US dealt with tribal nations as sovereign parties and signed roughly 370 ratified treaties with them — formal, negotiated recognition of ownership.

2/ 1870 to 1880 is the collapse. Railroads, gold strikes and the Plains wars ran through it. In 1871 Congress ended treaty-making with tribes altogether; after that, land changed hands by statute and executive order, with no negotiation required.

3/ Then the quiet mechanism. The 1887 Dawes Act broke reservations into individual family plots and declared the leftovers “surplus” for sale to settlers. Tribal holdings fell from about 138 million acres in 1887 to roughly 48 million by 1934.

4/ That is why the 2022 panel is dots rather than blocks. Allotment didn't only shrink reservations, it perforated them — producing the checkerboard of tribal, individual and non-Native title inside single reservations that still snarls jurisdiction today.

5/ Allotment ended with the Indian Reorganization Act of 1934. Today roughly 56 million acres are held in trust, on the order of 2% of US land. The Navajo Nation alone runs to about 27,000 square miles — larger than West Virginia.

6/ Language survived unevenly. This map gives the most-spoken Native language by state: Navajo leads nationally with something near 170,000 speakers, Yup'ik dominates Alaska, Ojibwe holds the northern Midwest. (Several labels are misspelled.)

7/ Cherokee's wide eastern spread is a reminder to read carefully — “most spoken” in a state can mean a few hundred people. Of roughly 170 Native languages still spoken in the US, most have well under 1,000 speakers left.
